meta.outcome: Create generic functions, interfaces, and utility types from scratch.

objectives.title: Author generic functions and use built-in utility types.

Easy.q: What does the `<T>` signify in this TypeScript function?
options: It declares a Type Variable (Generic), allowing the function to accept and return any type while maintaining strict type safety
It is a syntax error in JavaScript
It casts the argument to a string
It means the function returns a Promise
Easy.a: It declares a Type Variable (Generic), allowing the function to accept and return any type while maintaining strict type safety
Easy.explanation: Generics allow you to write reusable components that work with a variety of types rather than a single one, while still giving you perfect autocomplete.

Easy.scenario: You are creating an API testing utility that parses JSON responses. The response structure changes depending on the endpoint.
Easy.q: How do Generics help in this scenario?
options: You can pass the expected Interface as a Generic type parameter, so the returned data is correctly typed
Generics automatically mock the API response
Generics make the API request faster
Generics bypass CORS errors
Easy.a: You can pass the expected Interface as a Generic type parameter, so the returned data is correctly typed
Easy.explanation: By calling `fetchData<UserResponse>()`, TypeScript knows the result matches the UserResponse shape.

Medium.q: How would you correctly instantiate this type for an API returning a `string` payload?
options: let res: ResponseData<string>;
let res: ResponseData(string);
let res: ResponseData = string;
let res<string>: ResponseData;
Medium.explanation: You pass the type argument inside angle brackets `< >` when using the generic interface.

Medium.scenario: A developer writes a generic function but TypeScript complains because they try to call `arg.length`, and TypeScript doesn't know if the generic `T` has a length property.
Medium.q: How can you fix this using Generic Constraints?
options: Change `<T>` to `<T extends { length: number }>`
Cast arg to `any`
Change the generic to `<T = length>`
Remove the generic entirely
Medium.explanation: The `extends` keyword in a generic declaration enforces a constraint, ensuring the passed type meets specific minimum requirements (like having a length property).

Hard.q: What sophisticated type-safety mechanism is being used here?
options: The compiler is enforcing that the requested 'key' strictly exists as a property name on the generic object 'T'
It is converting the object into an array of keys
It is making the property optional
It is a runtime validation check
Hard.a: The compiler is enforcing that the requested 'key' strictly exists as a property name on the generic object 'T'
Hard.explanation: Using `K extends keyof T` is an advanced TypeScript pattern that guarantees you cannot ask for a property that doesn't exist on the object, preventing undefined errors at compile time.

Easy.q: Why are Playwright fixtures generally preferred over standard beforeEach hooks?
options: Fixtures establish strong isolation and explicit dependency injection per test
Fixtures are exactly the same as beforeEach hooks
Fixtures run asynchronously while hooks are synchronous
Fixtures only run once per test suite
Easy.a: Fixtures establish strong isolation and explicit dependency injection per test
Easy.explanation: Fixtures provide independent, isolated environments for each test, avoiding shared state issues.

Medium.q: What happens to the page fixture after a test block finishes executing?
options: Playwright automatically tears down the isolated Browser Context and closes the page, ensuring a clean slate for the next test.
The page remains open and is reused by the next test in the file.
The developer must manually call await page.close() or memory leaks will occur.
The entire Browser executable is killed and rebooted.
Medium.a: Playwright automatically tears down the isolated Browser Context and closes the page, ensuring a clean slate for the next test.
Medium.explanation: Built-in fixtures like page are bound to the lifecycle of the test. Playwright handles the teardown automatically, guaranteeing that no cookies, local storage, or DOM state bleed into the next test.

Hard.q: Why might a Senior SDET choose to manually inject the browser fixture and create their own context, instead of just using the default page fixture?
options: Because they need to simulate a multi-tab or multi-user scenario (e.g., User A and User B interacting simultaneously in separate isolated sessions).
Because the default page fixture does not support JavaScript.
Because the browser fixture executes tests 50% faster.
Because the page fixture cannot handle await page.goto().
Hard.a: Because they need to simulate a multi-tab or multi-user scenario (e.g., User A and User B interacting simultaneously in separate isolated sessions).
Hard.explanation: The default page fixture provides a single, isolated context. If you are testing a real-time chat application and need two users logged in simultaneously with different cookies, you must inject the raw browser fixture and instantiate multiple distinct contexts manually.

Easy.q: In this custom fixture, what does the `use()` function do?
options: It pauses the fixture and hands execution control over to the actual test block, passing the initialized data
It deletes the page object
It throws an error if the test fails
It runs an assertion
Easy.a: It pauses the fixture and hands execution control over to the actual test block, passing the initialized data
Easy.explanation: The `use()` callback is the boundary between the Setup phase and the Test phase. Calling it 'yields' the execution to the test.

Easy.scenario: You have created a custom fixture called `databaseConnection`. You want a specific test to utilize it.
Easy.q: How do you request this fixture in your test?
options: Simply add `{ databaseConnection }` to the test function arguments
Call global.databaseConnection
Import it directly from the file
Use the --fixture CLI flag
Easy.a: Simply add `{ databaseConnection }` to the test function arguments
Easy.explanation: Playwright uses Dependency Injection. You just destructure the name of the fixture in the argument list, and Playwright dynamically initializes it for you.

Medium.q: If the test fails, does the 'Teardown' code still execute?
options: Yes. Code placed after `use()` is guaranteed to execute during the teardown phase, regardless of test pass/fail status
No, the worker crashes immediately
Only if you add a try/catch block
Yes, but it runs before the test ends
Medium.a: Yes. Code placed after `use()` is guaranteed to execute during the teardown phase, regardless of test pass/fail status
Medium.explanation: Fixtures natively handle safe teardown. The engine ensures the block after `use()` runs so you can clean up databases or close connections safely.

Medium.scenario: You want your custom `adminPage` fixture to execute automatically for every single test in the file, even if the test doesn't explicitly request it in the arguments.
options: Set `auto: true` in the fixture options definition
You cannot do this; fixtures must always be requested
Put it in the test.describe
Name the fixture 'global'
Medium.a: Set `auto: true` in the fixture options definition
Medium.explanation: You can define automatic fixtures by passing an array syntax: `adminPage: [ async ({}, use) => { ... }, { auto: true } ]`. These act like transparent beforeEach hooks.

Hard.scenario: A Senior SDET argues that Fixtures are architecturally superior to standard Page Object Models instantiated in `beforeEach` hooks.
Hard.q: What are the primary architectural benefits of Playwright Fixtures? (Select all that apply)
options: Lazy loading: Fixtures only instantiate if a test specifically requests them, saving execution time
Encapsulated teardown: Fixtures handle their own cleanup safely without needing a separate `afterEach` block
Global State: Fixtures share the exact same variable instance across all tests in parallel
Composability: Fixtures can depend on other fixtures to build complex dependency trees safely
a: Lazy loading: Fixtures only instantiate if a test specifically requests them, saving execution time
Encapsulated teardown: Fixtures handle their own cleanup safely without needing a separate `afterEach` block
Composability: Fixtures can depend on other fixtures to build complex dependency trees safely
Hard.explanation: Fixtures are isolated per-test, they do NOT share global state (which is a good thing!). They excel in lazy evaluation, encapsulation, and tree-like composability.

Medium.q: Why is composing fixtures hierarchically an important architectural pattern?
options: To prevent test flakiness
Because Playwright requires it
To make tests slower
It is optional

Hard.q: Which fixture anti-pattern causes database deadlocks during parallel teardown?
options: Using global state across tests
Using test.beforeEach
Using web-first assertions
Using page.goto
Hard.scenario: You are auditing a failing test suite focused on this module's core topic.
